documents.title: Student Guidance FAQ on Generative AI
tiers: No AI use allowed (human brains only)
AI Friendly assignment (use responsibly and cite appropriately)
documents.summary: Student-facing FAQ saying Marquette has no university-wide AI policy and that instructors set rules in the syllabus, using three assignment labels. It adds a no-assumption rule when the syllabus is silent, ties unattributed or unapproved AI use to the Honor Code and plagiarism, and covers privacy, learning, and career reasons.
documents.stance_why: The FAQ states "Marquette does not have a university-wide policy" and "In general, instructors decide on AI use for your courses", and lists assignment labels ("No AI use allowed", "AI use limited", "AI Friendly assignment"); it sets no single stance and hands the decision to instructors, so delegates with tiers.

units.why: The page opens by saying Marquette "calls students to use AI tools responsibly and ethically", a general principle that frames the guidance; coded as an institution-level framework (P56) with a student actor because it addresses students, informs because it states a principle rather than a rule.
units.anchor: Marquette calls students to use AI tools responsibly and ethically.

units.why: "our Jesuit values challenge students to approach AI with discernment" states a mission-based principle for AI use; it is a framework statement (P56) rather than a harm or rationale-for-skill claim, so P53 and P41 fit less well.
units.anchor: our Jesuit values challenge students to approach AI with discernment.

units.why: "Review each course syllabus for rules on AI use" tells students the syllabus is where the rule lives, so the rule is set per course/instructor (P04); actor is student and phase course-start.
units.anchor: Review each course syllabus for rules on AI use.

units.why: The sentence lists three assignment labels, "No AI use allowed (human brains only)", "AI use limited (within guidelines)" and "AI Friendly assignment", which are named tiers of AI use (P05); it only says "Some instructors will" use them, so modality is informs and the stance is neutral.
units.anchor: AI use limited (within guidelines)

units.why: "When assignment instructions are unclear or you are uncertain about using AI, consult the May I Use AI for Classwork? decision tree" directs unsure students to a tool; closest type is P10 (when unsure, check first) although it points to a decision tree before the instructor.
units.anchor: When assignment instructions are unclear or you are uncertain about using AI
units.frag_end: appropriate and inappropriate uses of AI in your coursework.

units.why: "Marquette does not have a university-wide policy" states that no single institutional rule exists, so the decision is left to others; P04 fits (decided per instructor) and the statement is informational.
units.anchor: Marquette does not have a university-wide policy.

units.why: "In general, instructors decide on AI use for your courses" explicitly assigns the decision to instructors, the defining case of P04.
units.anchor: instructors decide on AI use for your courses.

units.why: "The college or department offering your course may have its own AI guidelines" adds another level of rule-setting beyond the instructor; coded under P04 (who decides) as it says the rule can come from the unit, not the university.
units.anchor: The college or department offering your course may have its own AI guidelines.

units.why: "If a tool creates or transforms your work, it's generative AI" defines what counts as AI for the guidance, which is a definition of scope (P61).
units.anchor: If a tool creates or transforms your work, it's generative AI.
units.frag_start: If a tool creates or transforms

units.why: "some long-standing software, such as word processors and spelling/grammar checkers, have revamped into AI tools" widens the definition to everyday software, so it sets scope (P61); P07 is about rules for built-in AI in editors, and this passage states no rule.
units.anchor: word processors and spelling/grammar checkers, have revamped into AI tools.

units.why: "If in doubt, check with your instructor" tells students unsure whether a tool counts as AI to ask the instructor, which is P10 (ask first).
units.anchor: If in doubt, check with your instructor.

units.why: "If allowed by your instructor, AI can help you brainstorm ideas, summarize course content and explore new perspectives" names permitted uses conditional on instructor permission; brainstorming is the lead use so P15 (summarizing would be P14), modality may.
units.anchor: AI can help you brainstorm ideas, summarize course content and explore new perspectives.
units.frag_start: If allowed by your instructor, AI

units.why: "AI may short-circuit your learning, if it replaces critical thinking or problem solving" warns that AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: AI may short-circuit your learning, if it replaces critical thinking or problem solving.
units.frag_start: But AI may short-circuit your learning

units.why: "AI can yield inaccurate or biased information" says output may be wrong or biased, which is the P31 warning to verify output.
units.anchor: AI can yield inaccurate or biased information.
units.frag_start: Keep in mind that AI can

units.why: "AI misuse may lead to academic integrity issues" links misuse to the integrity process, i.e. misuse is treated as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: AI misuse may lead to academic integrity issues.

units.why: "Is this use helping me learn or replacing the work I am meant to do?" is a self-check prompt telling students to keep doing the work themselves, matching P32 (student stays the primary problem-solver).
units.anchor: Is this use helping me learn or replacing the work I am meant to do?
units.frag_end: work I am meant to do?

units.why: "Does the final work still reflect my own thinking, voice and values?" asks students to ensure submitted work is their own, which is P29 (ownership of what is submitted).
units.anchor: Does the final work still reflect my own thinking, voice and values?

units.why: "would I feel comfortable explaining how I used AI to my instructor?" asks students to be ready to explain their use; nearest type is P30 (be able to explain), though it concerns explaining use rather than every line.
units.anchor: would I feel comfortable explaining how I used AI to my instructor?
units.frag_start: Does my course syllabus give me

units.why: "Struggle and effort are part of learning. AI should support learning, not skip it." explains that skipping the work undermines learning, which is P41.
units.anchor: AI should support learning, not skip it.

units.why: "Pause before you outsource work to AI, escaping the learning process" asks students to stop before delegating work to AI; it is about keeping the learning process, P41, and the preceding line says to seek human support first.
units.anchor: Pause before you outsource work to AI, escaping the learning process.

units.why: "Marquette recommends reaching out to campus resources" (instructor, Ott Writing Center, Raynor Library, Academic Resource Center) advises seeking human support before consulting AI; no existing type covers directing students to human help first.
units.anchor: Marquette recommends reaching out to campus resources
units.uncovered_note: Advises students to use human campus support services (instructor, writing center, library, ARC) before consulting AI.

units.why: "Start with the AI Tool List, noting which tools are available to students" points students to a university list of tools available to them, i.e. sanctioned tools (P17).
units.anchor: noting which tools are available to students.

units.why: "Do not enter personal, confidential or sensitive information into public AI tools" is a data-protection prohibition (P50).
units.anchor: Do not enter personal, confidential or sensitive information into public AI tools.

units.why: "you may lose control of your data when you enter into a public AI tool" explains the privacy risk behind the previous rule, still P50 as an informing statement.
units.anchor: may lose control of your data
units.policy: Students may lose control of their data when they enter it into a public AI tool, which could reuse the data to answer questions asked by anyone else.

units.why: "Follow guidance from your instructor or faculty researcher on approved and supported AI tools" tells students to use only approved, supported tools as directed, matching P50 (prefer vetted tools).
units.anchor: Follow guidance from your instructor or faculty researcher on approved and supported AI tools.

units.why: "not all AI platforms protect your data in the same way" is a privacy fact that supports choosing vetted tools (P50).
units.anchor: not all AI platforms protect your data in the same way.

units.why: "Ask your instructor before using AI for your classwork" is the instruction when the syllabus is silent; it is an ask-first rule (P10), while the next line gives the fallback rule (P06).
units.anchor: Ask your instructor before using AI for your classwork.

units.why: "Don't assume omission of AI from the syllabus means you can use AI" sets what applies when the syllabus is silent: no assumed permission, i.e. the fallback rule (P06).
units.anchor: Don't assume omission of AI from the syllabus means you can use AI.

units.why: "Using AI (without instructor approval) is not individual work" ties unapproved AI use to an Honor Code breach ("neither to accept nor give unauthorized help"), i.e. classes it as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Using AI (without instructor approval) is not individual work.

units.why: "submitting AI work as your own is plagiarism" classifies passing off AI work as plagiarism, i.e. misconduct (P36); P19 would be about having AI produce work, which this does not state outright.
units.anchor: submitting AI work as your own is plagiarism.

units.why: The quoted Academic Misconduct Policy defines plagiarism as "lacking or unclear attribution of content developed with generative software", making unattributed AI content misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: lacking or unclear attribution of content developed with generative software
units.policy: Plagiarism includes the use of another's creations or ideas without proper attribution, including lacking or unclear attribution of content developed with generative software ('artificial intelligence').

units.why: "To avoid academic misconduct, disclose and attribute AI use" directly requires disclosure and attribution (P24) as the way to stay within integrity rules.
units.anchor: To avoid academic misconduct, disclose and attribute AI use.

units.why: "You are obliged to report any observed breaches of this honor code" requires students to report peers' misconduct; no type covers reporting by other students.
units.anchor: to report any observed breaches of this honor code and academic honesty.
units.frag_start: The Honor Code is clear. You
units.uncovered_note: Students are obliged to report observed honor-code breaches by other students (peer reporting).

units.why: "The form includes an option to remain anonymous" describes how peers can report suspected misuse via the Academic Misconduct Report Form; peer reporting channel is not covered by any type.
units.anchor: The form includes an option to remain anonymous.
units.uncovered_note: Channel for students to report suspected misconduct, including anonymous reporting.

units.why: "Your instructor specifies which citation style to use for attribution" says how AI attribution is done, left to the instructor; it belongs with disclosure (P24).
units.anchor: Your instructor specifies which citation style to use for attribution.

units.why: "Using AI in ways not permitted by your instructor may violate Marquette's academic integrity policies" ties unpermitted use to integrity violations (P36).
units.anchor: may violate Marquette’s
units.frag_start: Using AI in ways not permitted

units.why: "It's important to follow each instructor's direction about AI in your course" makes the instructor the authority for each course (P04).
units.anchor: follow each instructor's direction about AI in your course.

units.why: "learning how to use AI responsibly now prepares you to: Collaborate effectively with technology" gives a career/skills reason for learning responsible AI use (P44).
units.anchor: learning how to use AI responsibly now prepares you

units.why: "Use tools in ways that honor human dignity and social responsibility" states an ethical principle of AI use; it is a value framework (P56), not a named harm (P53).
units.anchor: Use tools in ways that honor human dignity and social responsibility

units.why: "AI will be part of many professions you enter after graduation" is a career rationale that responsible AI use is a professional skill (P44).
units.anchor: AI will be part of many professions you enter after graduation.

units.why: "Employers expect not just technical skill but judgment, ethics and accountability" gives an employer-expectation rationale for responsible AI use (P44).
units.anchor: Employers expect not just technical skill but judgment, ethics and accountability.

units.why: "AI can be a helpful learning tool, but it is not a substitute for your thinking" keeps the student as the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: it is not a substitute for your thinking.

documents.title: AI, Generative and Emerging Technologies Support for the Classroom
documents.summary: Center for Teaching and Learning page for instructors stating Marquette has no unified AI policy and encouraging instructors to tell students their own expectations. It lists related guidance documents and offers department presentations and videos; the page itself does not set a stance.
documents.stance_why: The page says "Marquette does not have a unified AI policy in favor of instructional flexibility" and asks instructors to articulate "what you encourage, what you prohibit, and what you find acceptable", so it sets no stance itself and delegates.

units.why: "Marquette does not have a unified AI policy in favor of instructional flexibility" says there is no single policy and that flexibility is preferred, so instructors decide (P04).
units.anchor: Marquette does not have a unified AI policy in favor of instructional flexibility

units.why: "your college or department may have its own guidelines" notes that rules can also be set at college or department level, a who-decides statement (P04).
units.anchor: your college or department may have its own guidelines

units.why: "students need and deserve clear articulations of what your expectations are" tells instructors to state their AI expectations to students, i.e. an AI statement (P09).
units.anchor: students need and deserve clear articulations of what your expectations are

units.why: "Recommended communication with students can be found below" points instructors to suggested syllabus language and visuals for communicating AI expectations (P09).
units.anchor: Recommended communication with students can be found below.

units.why: "There are multiple policies surrounding the use of AI that are important and relevant" introduces a set of institutional guidance documents (faculty discernment guide, ITS responsible use guidelines, academic integrity director recommendations), which is a framework pointer (P56).
units.anchor: There are multiple policies surrounding the use of AI that are important and relevant

units.why: "offers customized sessions on AI resources, responsible use, course design considerations, and department-level discussions" is support for faculty to learn about AI and plan policy (P63).
units.anchor: offers customized sessions on AI resources, responsible use, course design considerations
units.frag_start: The Center for Teaching and Learning,

units.why: The "Our Favorite Things" video series features faculty and students "reflecting on how they are both discerning and may be engaging AI", supporting faculty in learning from peers (P63).
units.anchor: reflecting on how they are both discerning and may be engaging AI
units.frag_end: Ignatian Pedagogy and our Jesuit mission.

documents.title: Academic Integrity
documents.summary: Provost academic integrity page. On AI it asks instructors to talk to students before filing an allegation, to give specific examples of unattributed generative material, and to treat AI detectors as unreliable. It sets no stance on AI use itself.
documents.stance_why: The page gives only integrity-process guidance (e.g. "AI detectors offer both false positives and false negatives") and no rule on whether students may use AI, so it sets no stance and delegates.

units.why: "We encourage all instructors to speak with their students about potential allegations before submission" asks instructors to talk with the student before filing a report, which is P57.
units.anchor: speak with their students about potential allegations

units.why: "Ignatian pedagogy is founded on person-to-person presence" is the stated reason for talking with students before reporting, so it explains P57.
units.anchor: Ignatian pedagogy is founded on person-to-person presence.

units.why: "ensure that your report includes explicit rationales with specific examples of what you suspect to be unattributed material" sets what an AI-related misconduct report must contain; treated as part of the integrity process (P36).
units.anchor: ensure that your report includes explicit rationales with specific examples

units.why: "AI detectors offer both false positives and false negatives, so their findings as evidence of misconduct are less reliable" says detectors are unreliable as proof, which is P39.
units.anchor: offer both false positives and false negatives

notes: Responsible-use PDF screened exclude, not coded. Policy fields left null where the anchor fully states the rule. Peer-reporting units and the 'human campus resources first' advice are UNCOVERED.
